183613:
Testimony Adam Nordell in SUPPORT of LD 130
An Act to Establish the PFAS Response Program and to Modify the Fund To Address PFAS
Contamination
Good morning, Senator Talbot-Ross, Representative Pluecker and distinguished members of
the Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry Committee,
My name is Adam Nordell. I am a campaign manager for Defend Our Health and a PFAS
impacted farmer. l also served on two sub-committees which helped draft rules to govern
DACF's PFAS Fund. Please accept my testimony in support of LD 130.
DACF staff have now identified more than 80 sludge spread farms where PFAS contamination
exceeds soil screening standards and/or Maine's drinking water standard. Of those farms, a small handful have been forced out of business by the contamination. That financial risk could
easily extend to all impacted farms in our state. Thanks to the hard work of DACF staff, the vast
majority of these impacted farms have been able to pivot and responsibly continue operating.
DACF has helped farmers conduct soil, water, crop & livestock sampling. The Department has made investments in equipment and infrastructure to help the farms produce low risk crops. DACF has delivered clean irrigation water as a short term support while investing in high volume filtration and new wells. DACF has provided PFAS-free hay to farmers whose fields are contaminated and identified successful strategies to get the PFAS out of beef and dairy herds.
There's more work to do. We know that PFAS do not break down in the environment, and as such, they will remain a risk for Maine's farms far into the future. We know that the Department
is not yet working with all the contaminated farms. For example, DEP's PFAS investigation
excludes numerous farms spread with composted sludge. The investigation does not include
farms impacted by AFFF fire fighting foam, but the Department of Defense has identified 53 Maine farms at risk of contamination. On one of those sites, groundwater levels exceed 80,000 parts per trillion (ppt) for the chemical PFOS alone. Maine's safe drinking water standard is 20 ppt, and the national drinking water standard is 4 ppt. If we are invested in the safety of our food supply and the health of Maine's farming community, we should pass LD 130 so DACF can
continue working with all impacted farmers.
l especially appreciate the language authorizing the Department to work with CDC to establish
maximum limits on PFAS in foods based on updated understanding of the chemicals' toxicology.
Impacted farmers can use these to demonstrate to their customers that they have succeeded in producing food that is under the threshold, and therefore safe for even/one to enjoy.
The committee should support DACF's ongoing efforts to mitigate the risks posed by PFAS to our farming community by passing LD 130.
Thank you for your consideration
Adam Nordell, Defend Our Health 565 Congress Street, Suite 204, Portland, ME 04101.
10032197:
Adrienne Lee Knox LD 130
Good Morning. Distinguished members of the Maine Legislature's Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry Committee..My name is Adrienne Lee. My husband Ken Lamson and I own and operate New Beat Farm in Knox, Maine, Waldo County. Thank you for the opportunity to speak today. I am testifying in support of LD130.
Our farm is comprised of 94 acres of fields and forest and we have been farming this land since 2012, growing MOFGA Certified Organic Produce and Cut flowers for our local community through farmers markets and wholesale outlets. Three years ago we discovered that some of our farmland, irrigation and well water were contaminated with high levels of PFAS. This discovery put us in a tailspin trying to figure out if we could find a viable path forward farming this land as well as processing the fact that our family all had very high levels of PFAS in our bodies.
The only reason that I can speak to you today, and talk about our farm in the present tense, is due to the States creation of the PFAS Fund and the work that DACF has done to support Maine farmers who are dealing with PFAS. At this point, three years post discovery, our farm is still on shaky ground but with support of resources from the PFAS Fund, we have identified ways that our farm can find a economically viable path forward and continue to provide our community with safe and nutritious food. We have received support from the PFAS Fund in a variety of ways. That being said, we know that by staying farming on this land that we will forever be dealing with these "Forever Chemicals". Making farming "work" while managing PFAS will be an ongoing, ever evolving process. We are not alone in that, and in that vein it seems critical that the work of the PFAS Fund should be built into a more permanent PFAS Response Program for the State.
Along with being an affected farmer I also sit on the PFAS Fund Advisory Committee and have helped to develop the programs that have been put in place. Figuring out how to properly address this complex issue has been no small task, and the Fund and DACF have learned some things along the way as to how best to support both farmers and Ag adjacent community members affected by PFAS. In that vein I urge you to support the Department recommended improvements to the PFAS Fund and support this bill as written to maintain vital assistance for Maine's agricultural community. Sincerely, Adrienne Lee New Beat Farm Knox, ME
10032179:
Eben Sumner West Baldwin LD 130
Good afternoon Senator Talbot - Ross, Representative Pluecker, and the distinguished members of the Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry. My name is Eben Sumner, I'm from West Baldwin, Maine. I am the co-founder of TerraGenix, a company focused on PFAS soil remediation using industrial hemp.
I am also a concerned citizen regarding Maine's agricultural and environmental future. I strongly support the establishment of the PFAS Response Program and the modifications to the Fund to Address PFAS Contamination, as outlined in this bill. Protecting our farms, food supply, and public health from the risks associated with PFAS contamination is critical. Equally as important to protecting Maine's citizens is the need to address clean up of these harmful, forever chemicals are already posing such a sever risk.
I appreciate that this bill not only creates a comprehensive response to address and mitigate PFAS contamination but also includes important financial support measures to assist affected commercial farms, and cleanup. I believe that the integration of testing support, technical assistance, and on-farm mitigation and remediation strategies will help our agricultural producers maintain viable operations and safeguard our communities.
That said, I do have a couple of important questions regarding the implementation details of this bill:
The bill requires the establishment of an advisory committee, with two co-chairs drawn from its members. Could you clarify how the composition of this committee will be determined? Specifically, who will select the members, and what criteria or process will be used to ensure that the committee represents the diverse perspectives of our agricultural producers, public health experts, and local communities? The bill also mentions that financial assistance will be provided to PFAS-impacted agricultural producers for testing, on-farm remediation and mitigation, and other necessary adjustments. While I understand that proceeds from the sale or lease of contaminated property will be deposited into the Fund, could you elaborate on how sustainable and sufficient this funding source is expected to be? In other words, what measures are in place to ensure that this financial support will consistently meet the needs of affected areas?
In closing, I want to reiterate my support for the bill. I believe that with clear guidelines on advisory committee formation and transparent funding mechanisms, Maine can lead the way in safeguarding and revitalizing both our agricultural industry and public health from the challenges of PFAS contamination.
Thank you for your time and consideration.

Respectfully submitted, Edward Nachamie

Maine's PFAS Fund, housed in the Department of Agriculture, Conservation & Forestry (DACF or
Department), is a robust response to the challenges facing Maine farmers confronted with PFAS contamination. With its comprehensive focus -- including site investigation and cleanup, scientific research on PFAS impacts on farm products and alternative crops, and addressing business impacts, health testing and monitoring -- it is a national model that has helped contaminated farm businesses
pivot management practices so they can stay in business and deliver safe food to Maine people. As the PFAS Fund moves from the planning stages to program implementation, it is important that the
Department has the tools it needs to effectively address the extraordinary range of challenges facing affected farms and farmers, and the food and agricultural sector of the State's economy.
LD 130 would house the PFAS Response Program within the Bureau of Agriculture, Food and Rural Resources as the ongoing response to farm contamination, including establishing and enforcing
Maximum Contaminant Levels (MCLs) of PFAS in farm products, and providing on-farm mitigation
strategies and financial assistance.
The Department has already established MCLs for milk and beef. LD 130 clarifies that authority and connects the MCLs to the PFAS Response Program's activities on farms by establishing baseline criteria for agricultural producers to comply with to access continued support. This ensures that there are clear standards in place for the Department's activities, whether providing technical or financial assistance, visiting a farm to take soil samples or other PFAS investigations, or making determinations that a farm product poses unacceptable risks to those consuming the food.
Not only does this approach protect consumers and provide assurances to the public that Maine's food system is safe and healthy, but it also establishes clear thresholds for accessing the safety net provided by the State as well as the MOFGA/Maine Farmland Trust emergency relief fund. Lacking these standards, farmers discovering that their farm products are contaminated with PFAS have been
left to their own devices, without guidance about whether they should pull those products from the marketplace or how to communicate with customers. LD 130 gives all farmers concrete
information on which to base these decisions and ensures a level playing field across Maine. It will
also protect farmers who don? pull their products from the marketplace, where they base their
decisions on the State standards establishing safe PFAS levels in food. LD 130 includes the opportunity for a hearing at the request of affected agricultural producers, providing due process and an opportunity for the farmer to appeal any decision to deny, cease or modify financial SU[JpOl't based on MCLs and other Department criteria.
While Maine remains at the forefront of PFAS response in the Nation, since the discovery of PFAS contamination of Maine farmland 2016, significant scientific and health risk information has been developed by the federal Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the federal Centers for Disease Control (federal CDC). Maine's Center for Disease Control and the State drinking water program have also been researching plant uptake of PFAS and safe food standards, and state and federal drinking
water standards for PFAS are being implemented across Maine. These new standards and risk assessments are now available to the Department as it moves ahead with setting food standards here in Maine; there is substantial scientific data now available to inform its actions.

In March 2024, EPA adopted national primary drinking water standards (MCLs) for PFOA, PFOS, PFHxS, PFNA, and HFPO-DA (commonly known as GenX Chemicals), as well as regulating mixtures containing two or more of PFHxS, PFNA, HFPO-DA, and PFBS.2 In addition, EPA issued a draft sewage sludge risk assessment in January 2025 finding that forever chemicals in sludge fertilizer pose cancer risk.3 EPA's sludge risk assessment found a significant cancer level of 1 in 1,000 (indicating that lifetime exposure to the carcinogenic pollutant would be expected to cause one additional case of cancer for every one thousand people in the exposed population) -- even under scenarios that it admitted "are not conservative estimates." Those most affected were people living on farms where PFAS-contaminated sludge was spread, and eating food grown on that land - in other words, farmers and their families.`
Conclusion: In summary, MOFGA supports LD 130 as an appropriate response in the year 2025 to PFAS contamination on Maine farms that we have been addressing in some form since 2016. It
makes sense to transition the DACF PFAS response to an ongoing program in the Bureau of
Agriculture, Food and Rural Resources. We wish we could see an end in sight, but the State is still
finding new sites contaminated with PFAS, and the need for technical and financial assistance for
farmers across Maine remains significant and ongoing. That being the case, assistance should be tied to compliance with food safety and other standards that are based on the best science and the most recent health data, with an opportunity for affected farmers to appeal adverse decisions and
understand the basis for any such decision. LD 130 will do just that and MOFGA urges the Committee
to unanimously vote "ought to pass."

Conservation, and Forestry Committee, I am Senator Henry Ingwersen, representing Senate District 32: Arundel, Biddeford, Dayton, Hollis, and Lyman, and l'm here before you today to

As this committee knows well, over the last few years, the Department of Agriculture,
Conservation, and Forestry has built a program to assist farmers impacted by the "forever chemical" PFAS. In the 2021 biennial budget, language was included and voted through by the

The department has been doing that by setting up the PFAS Response Program to help commercial farmers deal with PFAS contamination, and with the support of this committee, the legislature and many others, has created a Maine PFAS Response Program unmatched among all the other states.

assistance, and land acquisitions, among others.

testing to assess sources of contamination, crafting mitigation recommendations, and providing critical financial support to farms that can, in the Inaj ority of cases to date, allow them to
continue operating safely. The bill also enables DACF to establish the parameters for providing technical and financial assistance, including permitting DACF staff ongoing access to the

Farmers have had to deal with loss of income, possible health impacts, mental health impacts
due to stress and anxiety, and in some cases, farmers have had to completely shut down their
farm. Recognizing that the state needed to step in and provide assistance, in 2022 the Governor

MAINE FARMLAND TRUST

Testimony of Shelley Megquier, Policy & Research Director, Maine Farmland Trust, to the 132""
Legislature's Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry February 6, 2025
Good morning Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and members of the Joint Standing
Committee on Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry. My name is Shelley Megquier and I am the Policy & Research Director at Maine Farmland Trust (MFT). I am providing testimony on behalf of MFT in
support of LD 130 --An Act to Establish the PFAS Response Program and to Modify the Fund to Address PFAS Contamination.
MFT is a member-powered statewide organization that works to protect farmland, support farmers, and
advance the future of farming. Our goals are to keep agricultural lands working and help farmers and
their communities thrive. Since our founding in 1999, MFT has helped to permanently protect farmland
in every county in Maine, amounting to nearly 57,000 acres across 345 farms. Our Farm Network includes more than 550 farms that have participated in MFT's programming either through an agricultural easement or through one of our programs. Our main program areas are Farmland Protection, Farmland Access, Stewardship, Farm Business Planning, PFAS Support, Climate Resilience, and Policy and Research.
For the past several years, MFT has been deeply engaged in the strong and collaborative response to the
challenge of PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) contamination on Maine farms and farmland. The presence of PFAS in soil, water, crops and livestock is an emerging national issue, and PFAS
contamination in Maine continues to require a robust, coordinated response so we are adequately
supporting impacted farmers. To support immediate farmer's needs in the face of PFAS contamination,
MFT and MOFGA jointly established an Emergency Relief Fund, which continues to operate. MFT offers
resources and hands-on technical assistance to help farmers mitigate contamination and pivot their businesses, and partners with farmers on protected farms to navigate the terms of their easements with
as much flexibility as possible. MFT has also advocated in partnership with impacted farmers and other
organizations for a state policy response to ensure that impacted farmers receive the support they need -- helping to establish the PFAS Fund in 2022 that this bill seeks to reinforce.
State agencies have been working tirelessly to address the PFAS issue from a variety of different angles and DACF's PFAS Response Program has been a critical part of that response since it was created. LD 130 is necessary to ensure there is adequate statutory authority so DACF can continue to operate the PFAS Response Program in real time. As Program implementation continues, they will need the ability to create routine technical rules and other frameworks to ensure Maine's PFAS response remains comprehensive, informed by the needs of impacted farmers, and scientifically sound. LD 130 also makes some necessary housekeeping updates -- for example, stipulating that health care information be
treated as confidential, that new chairs of the advisory committee can be selected from among its members for a term of 2 years, and switching the number of required public meetings per year to one rather than remaining at two per year. These changes are reasonable, in our opinion, and aligned with the original intent of the program when it was created.
Thank you for the opportunity to provide testimony in support of LD 130. l'm happy to answer any
questions you may have.

Testimony in support of LD130 Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation & Forestry, My name is Arleigh Kraus. I reside in Warren. I am a co-founder of Terragenix, a Maine based PFAS remediation research company focused on hemp based solutions, I also have a small family farm. I am here today to express my strong support for LD 130 An Act to Establish the PFAS Response Program and to Modify the Fund To Address PFAS Contamination, which establishes the PFAS Response Program to protect Maine's agricultural producers, food supply, and public health from the devastating impacts of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) contamination. PFAS contamination has caused significant harm to Maine's farming communities, jeopardizing livelihoods, land, and confidence in our food system. This bill takes a necessary step in providing resources to mitigate PFAS contamination, support affected farmers, and establish guidelines for addressing this ongoing issue. The support of this legislation is essential to safeguarding Maine's agricultural future: Comprehensive PFAS Response Program: By creating a structured program within the Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry, this bill ensures that Maine has the tools to abate, clean up, and mitigate PFAS threats while providing direct support to affected farmers. Maximum PFAS Levels in Farm Products: Establishing science-based maximum PFAS levels in consultation with the Maine CDC and DHHS will help protect consumers and maintain the integrity of Maine's agricultural industry. Financial and Technical Assistance: Many farmers impacted by PFAS contamination face overwhelming financial burdens. This bill allows the state to provide necessary support, ensuring that affected farms can remain viable and continue contributing to our economy. Strategic Research and Policy Development: Addressing PFAS contamination requires continued research and data-driven decision-making. This legislation enables the state to invest in research that informs effective farm management and regulatory approaches. Responsible Land Management: The bill's modifications to the Fund To Address PFAS Contamination allow for the responsible management of contaminated agricultural properties, ensuring that resources are reinvested into PFAS mitigation efforts. Maine's farmers should not have to bear the cost of contamination they did not cause. This bill demonstrates our state's commitment to standing with our agricultural community, protecting public health, and ensuring a safe and sustainable food supply for all Mainers. I urge the Committee to support LD 130 An Act to Establish the PFAS Response Program and to Modify the Fund To Address PFAS Contamination and move it forward to passage. Testimony of Behalf of the University of Maine System Presented by Dr. Jason Bolton, Associate Dean of the University of Maine Cooperative Extension
In Support of LD130 - Formalizing the PFAS Response Program - February 6, 2025
Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation & Forestry: My name is Dr. Jason Bolton and I am the Associate Dean of the University of Maine Cooperative Extension and the PI of several congressional discretionary spending projects including the UMaine PFAS Analytical Detection Labratory and UMaine PFAS Research for Informing Farm Management Decisions. On behalf of the University of Maine System (UMS) and UMaine Extension, I am testifying in support of LD 130. This legislation will formalize the PFAS Response Program, which has resulted in collaborations between the University of Maine and the Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry (DACF) to support PFAS understanding, mitigation, and practices.
Since its inception, the PFAS Response Program has been crucial in addressing the challenges posed by per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) contamination. The collaboration between the DACF and the University of Maine has been instrumental in delivering scientific research, technical assistance, and direct farmer support. Through ongoing partnerships, the PFAS Response Program has contributed to:
 Conducting academic research on PFAS impacts, mitigation strategies, and long-term agricultural implications.
 Collaborating closely with DACF staff and affected farmers to implement best practices for monitoring and remediation.
 Establishing the UMaine PFAS Navigators program to guide farmers through complex regulatory, financial, and remediation challenges.
 Expanding PFAS laboratory capabilities to enhance testing, analysis, and data-driven policy recommendation
As Maine continues to address the challenges posed by PFAS contamination, we must maintain and strengthen the support structures available to our agricultural community. The passage of LD 130 will provide long-term stability for affected farmers and enable continued research and response efforts. We urge the committee to support this bill as written to preserve these vital resources.
Thank you for your time and consideration. We appreciate your commitment to Maine's agricultural future and look forward to continued collaboration on this critical issue.
Sincerely,
